entry.summary:

Saudi oil strikes out for the desert instead of the sea

🔹The insecurity of maritime routes and attacks on oil infrastructure have pushed Aramco to explore transferring Saudi oil overland to Oman and exporting it from the Arabian Sea coast.

🔹Saudi Arabia currently relies on two main routes to export its oil: the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea.

🔹Both routes have faced escalating security tensions in recent years, and attacks by Yemeni forces have driven up the cost and risk of oil tanker transit for Saudi Arabia.

🔹For this reason, Riyadh is seeking options to move oil overland through Saudi territory to a safer point before it reaches high-risk maritime routes.

🔹Saudi Arabia wants to transport part of its oil overland from the east of the country to a new outlet on the Arabian Sea coast, and from there ship it to Asian markets.

@Farsna - Link

entry.title: [ahmadzeidabad] What is Tehran's mayor really after? In some circles, the unprecedented assault…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @ahmadzeidabad

What is Tehran's mayor really after? In some circles, the unprecedented assault on Masoud Pezeshkian is seen as an attempt to force him to resign and install Alireza Zakani in his place! From every angle, the scheme and the intent behind it look foolish—but however foolish it may seem, that is no reason to rule it out in this country! The noisy spectacle Tehran's mayor has staged in recent days around "stabilizing the prices of essential goods," and the extensive propaganda support the Kayhan tribe has drummed up for him, show that something is going on beneath the surface and that a political agenda is being pursued! Even if stabilizing the prices of essential goods were possible and feasible, what business does it have with the mayor and the municipality? If the financial resources for such stabilization exist, the government should carry it out through subsidy payments; and if they don't exist, where is the municipality supposed to get them from? The municipality's revenue comes from the tolls it collects from the people. Is the plan to raise various tolls and use the difference to stabilize the prices of a handful of goods? At best, that amounts to taking from one pocket and putting into another! Is the municipality supposed to cover the cost of this stabilization by taking it from the government and other institutions? If the government or other institutions have such resources at their disposal, are their hands tied that Alireza Zakani should use their money to drum up political publicity for himself? During the 40-day war, people whose homes and dwellings had been destroyed by the fighting were housed for a time in Tehran hotels. Tehran's mayor presented this as his own feat of managing war refugees, when those hotels mostly belonged to the Mostazafan Foundation! Did the Tehran municipality pay for this housing, or did it use the Foundation's pocket to promote itself? In my view, the Mostazafan Foundation should come clean with the public about this. entry.title: [sadegh_alhosseini] Oil transit through Hormuz rises: The White House celebrated, the market didn't…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @sadegh_alhosseini

Oil transit through Hormuz rises: The White House celebrated, the market didn't buy it
Sadegh Al-Hosseini
Kelley Vlahos, editor of Responsible Statecraft, made important points in yesterday's article that I'll get into below. He says last week the White House and its supporters announced "the strait is open and we've won." On Sunday, however, Brent was still holding at $102. The gap between these two images is what this article is about.
What's really going on behind the numbers? Daily oil transit through Hormuz has reached 13 to 17 million barrels, down from about 20 million before the war. But a large portion of it is happening through an emergency workaround: state-owned ships pass through the strait with their tracking systems turned off and hand off their cargo to supertankers in safe waters. The cost of chartering a supertanker from the Persian Gulf to Asia has hit $1.2 million, insurance has gotten more expensive, and ships carrying fertilizer, aluminum, petrochemicals, and grain are still stranded in the Persian Gulf. America has sent a third aircraft carrier to the region, and its navy is, according to experts, stretched thin.
The drawdown from reserves is also heavy: 400 million barrels drawn from reserves in March, another 100 million barrels from the G7, America's strategic reserves at their lowest level since 1983, and JPMorgan saying it sees no end to this situation.
In other words, Iran can't fully close the strait, and America can't fully open it. Unless Trump reaches a deal with Iran; that's what the market is really waiting for.
Why is this news encouraging for us?
1. Trump's leverage has hit its ceiling. With three aircraft carriers, the strait has only become "half-open." When American experts themselves say the only way out is a deal with Iran, it means the military option costs more than it delivers.
2. The clock is working against the White House. The November midterm elections are approaching, and according to experts, fuel prices won't come down by then; the soaring cost of diesel has even hit American farmers. This pressure raises the incentive for a deal. But it's clear that the cost of this war is being paid by the people of Iran.
3. A deal would untie many knots at once. A world whose reserves have run dry is thirsty for fresh supply; it's not just oil — petrochemicals, fertilizer, and metals are also stuck behind this barrier.
The world has come to believe that Hormuz today is neither closed nor open; and the key is not on warships but on the negotiating table.
Full text of the article: https://responsiblestatecraft.org/hormuz-oil-transits-war/

entry.title:
[FarsNA] A mouth that opened at the wrong time
🔹In a clear pond, two ducks and a…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @FarsNA

A mouth that opened at the wrong time

🔹In a clear pond, two ducks and a turtle were neighbors, and a deep friendship and bond had formed between them. Time passed, and due to drought, the water in the pond began to dry up.

🔹The ducks, seeing that it was no longer possible to stay, came to the turtle to say goodbye and migrate to another body of water.

🔹The turtle lamented with sorrow and tears and said: "Waterlessness is far more dangerous for me, a slow-moving animal, than for you, and my life is impossible without any water. It is not the way of chivalry that you abandon me in this waterlessness; think of me and take me along with you."

🔹The ducks said: "Being apart from you is hard for us too, but you have a flaw: you take the advice of friends lightly and you don't shut your mouth at the right time!

🔹If you want us to take you too, there is one condition: we will bring a stick, we two will hold its two ends in our beaks, and you hold the middle of the stick firmly with your mouth so we can take flight. In the sky, no matter what people say and whatever shouts they raise, do not open your mouth!"

🔹The turtle promised and said: "I will obey and will not open my lips until the destination."

🔹The ducks brought the stick, the turtle gripped its middle firmly with its teeth, and they leapt into the air. As they were passing over a village, people's eyes fell on this amazing scene. An uproar rose among the people and they shouted: "Look! How the ducks are carrying the turtle through the air with a stick!"

🔹Hearing the clamor, the turtle could not endure it and became angry. Thinking it would say something to them, it opened its mouth and said: "May your eyes be blinded!"

🔹But as soon as it opened its lips, the stick was released from its mouth, and it fell from the height of the sky to the ground.

#حکایت@Farsna

You can listen to the recording of the launch event for Fukuyama's new book, titled "In the Realm of the Last Man," recently held at the London School of Economics and Political Science, here (file). The book traces the trajectory of his life, his positions, and his intellectual evolution over the past five decades. In it, Fukuyama explains how, under the influence of political and economic developments, he moved beyond the theory of the "End of History" and no longer sees the future of liberal democracy as guaranteed. Once known as one of the ideologues of the American right, he now considers himself a social democrat and stresses the need for wealth redistribution and stronger labor unions. He says he held two deep beliefs, both of which have been undermined by the developments of recent years: the belief that American military intervention can help spread democracy, and the belief in a maximally free market. The results of the American military attack on Iraq shattered the first belief, and the 2008 financial crisis shattered the second. He sees the rise of Trump in America as a sign of democracy's fragile state in the free market, and stresses that societies must have credible institutions to regulate the market and preserve democracy's institutional capacities.

Because moral propositions and ritual religious propositions differ from one another, including:▪️ 1. Rational justificationMoral rulings are capable of rational justification; one can explain what effect observing or not observing them has on human life.For example, reason understands that lying destroys trust, misleads others in decision-making, and damages human relationships. But reason alone does not understand what problems human life in general would face if we did not perform wudu or tayammum.▪️ 2. The bond among human beingsMorality can serve as the basis of a shared system for the life of all human beings; a system that helps their coexistence and compatibility. But rituals and rites do not create such a universal commonality and can also mark the boundary between followers of different religions and sects.▪️ 3. Conscience versus instructionMorality is related to the inner conscience of the human being; a person feels within themselves that good is preferable to evil. But knowledge of rituals and rites depends on instruction and cultural transmission.Imagine a fourteen-year-old adolescent who has not received religious instruction: they can understand the meaning of honesty — that is, harmony among beliefs, feelings, desires, speech, and action — and grasp its value; but they do not know prayer, tayammum, or the Eucharist without instruction.▪️ 4. Stability versus historical dependenceMoral values are not specific to a particular time, geography, ethnicity, or nation; but the form of rituals and rites depends on historical and cultural contexts.For example, the form and limits of religious covering and what is considered hijab have not been the same in different periods and societies. Ways of worship also differ among religious traditions. But the value of honesty does not change with a change of clothing, land, or historical period; harmony of speech and action and not deceiving others still has moral value.➖An excerpt from a private conversation among friends - Dey 96@mostafamalekian

The Islamic Republic 🇮🇷 executed Alireza Sepahi and Alireza Raeisi, two defendants in the "Alikhani Isfahan" case. Coinciding with the start of the World Week Against the Death Penalty, the judiciary of the Islamic Republic executed Alireza Sepahi and Alireza Raeisi, two of those arrested during the nationwide protests of Dey 1404, in the case known as "Alikhani Square." These two protesters were executed today, Monday 13 Mehr 1405, in Dastgerd Prison in Isfahan. Shahrzad Shahbazi, a lawyer and the defense attorney for Alireza Sepahi, wrote in this regard: "Alireza Sepahi's retrial was granted by the Supreme Court, but the parallel branch (Branch Two) of the Isfahan Revolutionary Court, without holding a hearing, rejected the retrial in less than 48 hours." Alireza Sepahi had previously been scheduled to be executed in the early hours of Tuesday, 6 Mordad 1405, along with Abolfazl Sepahi Badjani and Amirhossein Safari Hosseinabadi, but before being transferred to the execution site, he suffered a stroke and was taken to the hospital due to the severity of his physical condition. Two days later, after receiving medical treatment, he was returned to Dastgerd Prison in Isfahan. Published evidence regarding cases related to the Dey 1404 protesters shows that the death sentences issued so far have been accompanied by serious legal and juridical ambiguities, and in the vast majority of cases, the fundamental principles of a fair trial — including the right to effective access to a lawyer, public proceedings, independent examination of evidence, and full observance of the guarantees stipulated in the Code of Criminal Procedure — have not been observed. Therefore, the issuance and execution of death sentences against protesters, rather than being a sign of an independent and impartial judicial process, indicates that the death penalty has been turned into a tool for creating fear and terror in society and preventing the recurrence of protests. dadban4@mamlekate

An ordinary day! Yesterday I went to one of the public hospitals in central Tehran for an MRI. Even though I had booked an appointment in person in advance, I still waited two hours for my turn. During those two hours of waiting, verbal altercations broke out three times between hospital staff and patients or their companions, one of which nearly turned into a physical fight and made the atmosphere tense. Neither side in the disputes was at fault. Patients and their companions were demanding speed, accuracy, and respect, while the staff—due to the enormous volume and pressure of work on the one hand, and presumably low and inadequate wages on the other—had no patience for hearing complaints, and things escalated to disrespect and verbal altercation! If you sat and listened to the grievances of either side, you would acknowledge that they were right! This is not an exceptional situation in a public healthcare setting. It has become a completely ordinary matter. In some places, it even leads to physical fights, beatings, and sometimes murder. For God's sake, is this even a life? Let those who favor the continuation of sanctions, siege, and war answer! They, of course, do not consider sanctions, siege, and war to be a factor in creating these kinds of problems, and believe that all these problems stem from the president's inclination to negotiate with America and the failure to promulgate the hijab and chastity law. #احمد_زیدآبادی @ahmadzeidabad

entry.title:
[FarsNA] The consequence of befriending deceivers
🔹A crow, a wolf, and a jackal…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @FarsNA

The consequence of befriending deceivers

🔹A crow, a wolf, and a jackal lived in a thicket alongside a lion, and they got by on the leftovers of his kills.

🔹One day, a camel that had fallen behind from a caravan came to that thicket to graze. When the camel came upon the lion, it bowed, and the lion granted it safety, saying it could live in peace under his protection.

🔹Some time later, the lion was badly wounded in a fight with an elephant, collapsed in his cave, and lost the strength to hunt. The animals around him were left helpless with hunger. The crow, looking for a way out, proposed to his companions that they find a way to get the lion to eat the camel.

🔹The jackal said, "The lion has granted him safety, and breaking one's word is shameful." The crow replied, "Leave it to me; I'll devise a scheme so the camel himself walks into being sacrificed."

🔹The crow went to the lion and, with smooth talk, won him over and promised to arrange things so that there would be no need to break the covenant.

🔹Then he went to the wolf, the jackal, and the camel and said, "The Sultan's life is in danger; come, let us show our loyalty and offer ourselves. The lion does not eat our flesh, but the custom of service is fulfilled."

🔹They all went to the lion. First the crow stepped forward and offered himself, but the wolf and the jackal cried out, "You're scrawny and your flesh tastes foul!" Then the jackal volunteered, and the others called his flesh stinking. It was the wolf's turn, and they deemed his flesh harmful.

🔹The simple-hearted camel, seeing this staging, thought to himself that if he too made an offer, the companions would, following the same custom as before, come up with some excuse and the lion's protection would hold. So he came forward and said, "My body is a sacrifice for the Sultan; my flesh is pure and will fill everyone." No sooner had he finished speaking than all three animals said with one voice, "He speaks the truth!" and immediately fell upon him and made him their prey.

#حکایت@Farsna

Iran's water crisis is no longer a matter of the future; we see its signs today in the drying up of wetlands, land subsidence, and the depletion of groundwater reserves. Years of unchecked extraction from aquifers have consumed resources that, for many, may take decades or even centuries to replenish.

The book "Groundwater Governance: Developments and Advances" takes an interdisciplinary look at one of the most important yet least visible aspects of the water crisis: groundwater — resources that remain unseen, yet the lives, agriculture, and food security of communities depend on them.

By examining the experiences of various countries, this book demonstrates that protecting groundwater is not achievable through isolated projects alone; it requires scientific management, sound policymaking, and cooperation among government, local communities, and consumers.

▪️Iran's water crisis, rather than being a crisis of water scarcity, may be a crisis of water management.

✅ Documentary "Forgotten" Selected for the British Columbia Environmental Film Festival

🔹 The documentary "Forgotten," directed by Mehdi Afsharnik, has been selected for the official section of the British Columbia Environmental Film Festival (BCEFF) in Canada.

🔹 The festival, which focuses on environmental issues and the intersection of science, society, and documentary storytelling, will this year host works by environmental filmmakers and storytellers from around the world.

🔹 "Forgotten" tells the story of the state of Hawizeh Marsh and the crises that have affected this wetland on the Iran-Iraq border in recent years. Filmed in Iran, Iraq, and Turkey, the documentary explores the issues of water, dam construction, oil development, and their environmental and human consequences.

🔹 Mohammad Darvish, environmental activist and researcher, narrates the documentary, which seeks to transcend political borders and paint a picture of the many factors that have shaped the fate of one of the region's most important wetlands.

🔹 The online section of the British Columbia Environmental Film Festival will run from November 1 to 30, 2026, and its in-person program will take place on November 22 at the University of British Columbia (UBC).

#Virtual_Space_Roaming🔰Let's read the table so we don't become a mere shopfront🔺Maybe the development model is something other than buying Ronaldo!🔸Iran's young caravan — a nation that has been through war — in days when even coming and going through the skies was difficult for it, reached sixth place in Asia with 19 golds, 18 silvers, and 15 bronzes;◽It became the best country in West Asia by a wide margin◾It reeled in 6 more gold medals than the previous edition of the competitions◽Its girls claimed a 15-medal share of the caravan's 52 medals◾And it was only 3 more golds away from achieving the best result in its history...Hats off to them and may they stay in good health.🔸Saudi Arabia, too, reached twentieth place in the table with 3 golds, 2 silvers, and 9 bronzes — above Singapore and below Vietnam; it maintained the gap it has always had with Iran, and likely, with the rise of Iranian female athletes in recent years, that gap will only widen.🔸Of course, I have always avoided/avoid this kind of induction, but since for several years the most inefficient and backward development model — one that views every manifestation of development as a mere shopfront — has been used to humiliate Iranians, I say: Perhaps the "development model" should be something other than buying foreign players at ten times their market price for a seductive show in the domestic league... It is where the Portuguese Ronaldo cannot take the field in place of a Saudi athlete and win a medal that the true measure of nations' progress finally becomes clear... Just as in wartime, the true measure of a cheap military force — one whose software, hardware, and infantry arise from its own soil, science, and national awareness — is revealed against the world's greatest military power; and the impurity of an expensive army becomes apparent when, after being branded a "milking cow" and buying up countless fighter jets and Patriot systems and hiring hundreds of thousands of mercenaries from other countries, they are ultimately deployed to fight against a besieged land with the least possible military logistics — and get stuck in the mud.🔸Which problem does sports solve? To be honest, none! It was never supposed to solve any particular problem from the start, but it is a good mirror for reflecting a society's perception... If on the day our club team, worth about 15 million dollars, loses to a Saudi club team worth about 200 million dollars, we feel backwardness and humiliation — but when in a global event the gap between Iranian and Saudi national players reveals itself to this degree and we do not look at it "differently," it means that before anything else, we have lost the capacity for independent thinking — we too have become a shopfront!💬 Mohammad Sadegh Faramarzi🔘 Yes | Eitaa | Soroush+ | Instagram | Telegram@Kayhan_Online

Source: @darvishnameh

📝📝📝 The Shahnameh Becoming a Bestseller as a Sign of the Iranian People's Political Anxiety ✍️ Sina Jahanideh

✅ According to a report from one of the well-known publishers and bookstores, the best-selling book in Tehran's bookstores over the past few months has been Ferdowsi's Shahnameh. Those with greater financial means have bought Jalal Khaleghi-Motlagh's multi-volume critical edition, while those with lower incomes have settled for the single-volume Shahnameh of the Moscow print.

✅ This is happening at a time when book prices have risen sharply, and even 250- or 300-page books sometimes reach around one million tomans; as a result, the era of the physical book is more exposed to decline than ever before. In the year 1405, it seems that buying books, compared to previous years, has become a difficult and unnecessary matter for a large part of society. Yet right in the middle of this very crisis, the Shahnameh has become a meaningful exception.

✅ Perhaps this phenomenon cannot be explained merely by literary interest or a growing desire to read the Shahnameh. For some buyers today, purchasing the Shahnameh has become a kind of cultural-political ritual rather than merely the purchase of a book; as if at a moment when Iran, for many people, is exposed to political, geographical, and identity anxieties, the Shahnameh has become something more than a literary text: a condensed symbol of "Iran."

✅ From this perspective, buying the Shahnameh is a kind of symbolic act; an act in which the individual feels that by taking the book home, they are also preserving something of Iran. In this situation, the Shahnameh is no longer just a book to read; it becomes an object that must be had, kept, and passed on to the next generation. This is why even under conditions of the collapse of the book economy, the purchase of the Shahnameh can increase.

✅ Here the Shahnameh is a metaphor for Iran, and buying it can be a symbolic response to the fear of Iran's loss. Therefore, perhaps the Shahnameh becoming a bestseller under such conditions can be seen not as a sign of increased reading of the Shahnameh, but as a sign of increased political and identity anxiety; an anxiety that manifests itself in the form of buying a book, or more precisely, in the form of buying a symbol.

✅ From this perspective, the Shahnameh in the current situation is not just a book; it is the last refuge of the fetish of the book: a place where the book, at the moment of the decline of book-reading, takes on the burden of something far greater than itself; the burden of Iran.

🆔 @IranDel_Channel

entry.title: [mostafamalekian] 🔴 Why do even good things sometimes make us feel bad? ✍️ Mostafa…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @mostafamalekian

🔴 Why do even good things sometimes make us feel bad? ✍️ Mostafa Malekian

We usually assume that if good things happen to us, we'll feel good too. But the pleasantness of an event, in itself, doesn't guarantee that we can handle it well.

We live in a world that can be hard on us in two ways: not everything goes the way we want, and we have no certainty about what's coming.

▪️ The world has no obligation to fulfill our desires

There's no reason all the world's events should conform to our preferences and wishes. Some events are pleasant and some unpleasant; even a single event can make one person happy and another miserable.

Rain is a source of joy for a farmer waiting to water his field; but for a launderer who has hung washed clothes out to dry in the sun, it spells trouble.

The rain is the same rain; what differs is its relation to our desires and circumstances. The world has neither sworn to be our enemy nor promised to always go along with what we want.

▪️ Even joys may show up uninvited

The difficulty isn't just that we dislike certain events; it's also that we don't know what will come, or when.

Suppose you love someone dearly, but they show up at your door unannounced. Despite being happy to see them, you might lose your composure and fail to receive them the way you'd like.

Loving a guest is not the same as being ready for their arrival.

The same holds for the good things in life: we may want something, yet not be prepared for its sudden arrival. As a result, our reaction may be ill-considered and create fresh problems.

▪️ The suffering of the event and the suffering of the reaction

Part of life's difficulty comes from events not matching our desires; another part can stem from how we face them.

If we expect life to always unfold according to our wishes and predictions, we'll be constantly caught off guard. And being caught off guard can push us into reactions that only deepen our suffering.

So we must prepare ourselves to live in a world that holds both adversity and uncertainty—so that we can meet what arrives uninvited with greater composure.

We can't control the arrival of every uninvited guest; but we can learn how to face them.

📚 Mostafa Malekian | A conversation about the book "Welcoming the Unwelcome" by Pema Chödrön

@mostafamalekian

She described the charges brought in this case as "extremely serious." This alleged plot was thwarted at the same time as the Jewish High Holidays, the anniversary of last year's terrorist attack on the Heaton Park synagogue, and a rise in reports of antisemitic incidents across the UK. Two days before announcing these charges, the British government had accused the Islamic Republic of involvement in an attempt to sabotage Royal Air Force base Fairford. entry.title: [miladdokhanchi] For complex human problems, we shouldn't be looking for technical answers! If a…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @miladdokhanchi

For complex human problems, we shouldn't be looking for technical answers! If a pipe in your house bursts, that's a technical problem; but when your neighbor puts their trash out earlier than they're supposed to, that's no longer merely technical — it belongs to the realm of human problems. In teaching problem-solving, the first thing we draw the learner's attention to is distinguishing the technical problem from the human problem, and when we talk about problem-solving and teaching it, we mean the second category — because technical problems require expertise in their own field. If my phone stops working, I go to a specialist and they fix it. But human problems don't necessarily have predetermined solutions, and technical expertise alone won't help solve them. The solution to these problems has to be discovered, and solving them requires a basic understanding of the humanities and learning the skill of problem-solving. The biggest mistake is usually offering technical solutions for problems with human roots. When my employees' motivation is low and they show up late to work because of it, I can't force them into line with punishment, incentives, and a few new rules; I need to ask why their motivation has dropped, invite them into a conversation, and address the problem at the level of human relationships. Another mistake is assuming that our technical expertise can help us solve human problems — which it absolutely cannot. Yet another mistake is framing problems with human roots in technical terms. In that same example of lateness, if I say the reason is that they wake up late and that a morning phone call will get them to work on time, I've framed a human problem in technical terms! Mistaking technical problems for human ones and vice versa, offering technical solutions for human problems, and expecting clear technical solutions for complex problems — these are among the greatest plagues of our country's decision-making and problem-solving system. In this regard, the Iranian opposition abroad is hardly innocent either! We Iranians don't have strong problem-solving skills, and at the root of this situation you can feel the hegemony of engineers and physicians, the failure of humanities scholars to engage with concrete problems, and the jurists who want to solve human problems through technical legislation. This pattern shows itself when Hezbollahis are waiting for the leadership to solve the problem, the general public is waiting for the government, and some are waiting for Trump! Oblivious to the fact that solutions are discovered in small settings, and top-down solutions are all doomed to fail. Governments never have solutions for anything, and when they do, they're technical solutions for complex human problems. #Government-Addiction

The second issue of the specialized quarterly of the Payab Think Tank has been published.

🔴The Payab Quarterly, produced by the Payab Think Tank, aims to publish the opinions and initiatives of scholars in the fields of foreign policy, international relations, policymaking, and governance, following the style of journals based on policy reports.

🔷The editorial of this issue of the Payab Quarterly, titled "Political Psychology and International Relations," was written by Dr. Abbas Maleki, editor-in-chief of the Payab journal.

🔻This quarterly also features articles and notes including "The New Architecture of Strategic Relations with China and Russia: Authenticity and Comprehensive Capacity" by Dr. Mohammad Javad Zarif, "Sitting in Falsehood; or Wandering in the Wilderness? In Defense of Peaceful Nuclear Technology and a Third Way for Iran's National Security" by Dr. Hesamoddin Ashena, "Policymaking in Implementation; Rethinking Governance, Investment, and the Development of Iran's Oil and Gas Industry" by Dr. Gholamreza Manouchehri, "The Strait of Hormuz and the Dispute over Iranian Management" by Dr. Kourosh Ahmadi, "Foreign Policy and the Harmful Cycle of Decision-Making Expectation in Crisis Conditions" by Dr. Sasan Karimi, and "The Delegated and Unpredictable Iranian" by Dr. Seyed Jafar Hashemi.

🔻In the policy reports section, works have been published by Dr. Kiumars Ashtarian titled "The Right to Geography," Dr. Omid Asghari titled "Southophobia, the Right to Development, and Global Governance," Dr. Shafaei and Dr. Tabatabainejad titled "From the Strategy of Resistance to the Architecture of a New Order: The Question of Sustainable National Security," Dr. Mohammad Fekri titled "Opportunities and Risks of Post-War Street Gatherings," and Dr. Mohsen Shalbaf titled "The Rise of the Green Superpower; How Did China Surpass Europe and America in the Transition to Clean Technologies?"

🔻Further in the second issue of the Payab Quarterly, works by Amin Hasani, Amirparsa Garmsiri, Kasra Ghafouri, Mahya Danesh, Fatemeh Sadeghi Sheikh, and Ali Faryadras are also featured.

♦️The specialized Payab Quarterly, at 162 pages, is available for access and use by all interested parties on the Payab Think Tank website at www.paiab.org

entry.title: [jalaeipour] Thomas Schelling, the Nobel laureate in economics, once wrote that violence can…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @jalaeipour

Thomas Schelling, the Nobel laureate in economics, once wrote that violence can be the continuation of diplomacy by other means — a proposition that today applies to Iran-US relations more than ever. So much so that negotiations between the two countries are unfolding not in an atmosphere of trust, but under the shadow of war and threats, where force is not the opposite of diplomacy but has become part of its very logic. In this framework, Trump's approach to negotiation rests more on applying pressure and setting deadlines than on pursuing a win-win agreement. For him, negotiation is less a process for the gradual convergence of the parties and more a tool for dictating terms. Consequently, any sign of a tactical approach to negotiation aimed at buying time is read as stalling and can push the other side toward resorting to force. Indeed, the rationale behind the twelve-day war can be understood through this same logic. For America, that war was not an interruption of diplomacy but the driving force behind another round of negotiations. Now Washington, drawing on the battlefield and psychological outcomes of the war, has entered negotiations from a position it finds desirable — one in which red lines have been drawn by force and negotiation is merely about how to consolidate them. Under such circumstances, Iran does not face a simple choice. Accepting negotiation under the shadow of war can be construed as accepting the logic of pressure, while rejecting it carries the risk of heightened confrontation. What matters more than this binary is understanding how the nature of negotiation has changed: an agreement in such an atmosphere is not the product of confidence-building but the outcome of a perceived balance of power. On this basis, the ultimate question about the outcome of the negotiations is the very question Schelling raised: can the threat be contained and kept in the service of diplomacy, or has the logic of ultimatum and war reduced negotiation to a ceremonial affair? The answer to this question will determine the fate of Iran-US negotiations and the future of the region.@katechon6

entry.title: [Soroushdabbagh_Official] 13. Sohrab Sepehri was murmuring to himself somewhere in the "Traveler"…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @Soroushdabbagh_Official

13. Sohrab Sepehri was murmuring to himself somewhere in the "Traveler" notebook: "The journey carried me to equatorial lands / and beneath the shade of that tall green 'Banyan' / how well I remember / the phrase that entered the summer pasture of the mind: / Be vast, and alone, and humble, and hard." Sohrab, in his long-extended inner journey—which is of the nature of "horizontal wayfaring," setting out from oneself and arriving at oneself—draws back the curtain on his lived experience and pure illuminations; an experience that occurred beneath a towering tree, caught him unawares, drew him in, and like the Buddha enlightened him and granted him illumination. An experience that blew toward him and suffused every limb of his body and soul, marked a "rebirth" for him, and added to the volume of his "dove-like experiences"... Having breadth of spirit and a capacious digestive capacity makes you and me people of tolerance and civility, and noticeably increases our measure of "tolerance," "respecting the human being," and "accepting the other." Likewise, embracing "existential loneliness"—which is intertwined with your and my being—and reducing its volume with the aid of "velvety solitude," migrates lightness and joy toward us. "Humility and hardness" arrive together with high "self-esteem" and "self-worth" and are among the components of adequate mental health. "Humility" arrives with "realistic modesty," not "affected modesty." The modern wayfarer neither knows nor presents himself as lower than he is, nor considers and displays himself as higher than he is. He loves himself honestly and realistically, as he is, and with an eye to his endowments, capabilities, successes, weaknesses, misfortunes, and failures, deeply; and does not spend night and day seeking others' approval; rather, in Shamlou's phrase, he dwells at the "glorious altitude of humility" and fills and empties his lungs with its pure air. However, in "affected modesty," which is intertwined with low self-esteem, the individual does not believe in what he expresses about himself and in how he behaves, and with the affectation and artificiality that drips from his speech and behavior, he cunningly seeks to obtain others' approval. To the extent that you and I are "vast and alone and humble and hard," we are in a good state and experience mature dealings and relationships with the humans around us; for our existential goblet is filled, and following the Rendi of the Stoic-thinking Shirazi, we flow and drink and give drink.

Quoted from the book: Velvety Murmurs: Existential Whispers, Volume Two.
Author: Soroush Dabbagh

Farzaneh Fasihi, Iran's Olympic runner, responded to recent remarks by Ehsan Haddadi, head of the Athletics Federation of the Islamic Republic, calling him the "most notorious athlete in Iran's history" and writing that young athletes should treat him as a "cautionary tale," not a role model. In a text published on her Instagram page, Farzaneh Fasihi addressed Ehsan Haddadi, writing: "In your parallel world, you should have been behind bars and enjoyed no civil rights whatsoever, but what can we do — here they've handed the fate of hundreds and thousands of pure and innocent young people over to you, and now you've taken to lecturing." This reaction came after Ehsan Haddadi said in an interview with the state website "Varzesh 3" on Wednesday, 8 Mehr 1405, regarding female athletes: "I hold meetings with female runners and tell them you can become an influencer like many female athletes with 30,000, 50,000, 300,000 followers, or you can become a champion." Farzaneh Fasihi also wrote, referring to Reyhaneh Mobini, Zahra Zarei, and Fatemeh Mohiti-Zadeh, among Iran's female track and field athletes, that the thought of them wanting to follow Ehsan Haddadi's teachings is "like a nightmare" to her. She further addressed the head of the Athletics Federation, writing: "Being honorable has nothing to do with medals and championships. You have proven that even with a saddlebag full of medals, one can still go backward and become despised by a nation." Farzaneh Fasihi's reference to "behind bars" goes back to Ehsan Haddadi's judicial case in the 1390s. In that case, accusations of sexual assault and rape were brought against Ehsan Haddadi, and the court ruled for imprisonment, flogging, and a fine. However, the case was closed with the intervention of security institutions. In recent years, some prominent Iranian female track and field athletes have also left the country. Elnaz Kompani, Iran's record holder in the 60-meter hurdles, announced her emigration to America, and before her, Maryam Tousi, Iran's women's indoor 200-meter record holder, had emigrated to America.@VahidHeadline📡 @VahidOnline

entry.title:
[mohsenhesammazaheri] New micro-schools: mosque-schools and home-schools
In the second half of the…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @mohsenhesammazaheri

New micro-schools: mosque-schools and home-schools

In the second half of the 1990s, some households, arguing that schools were not religious enough, pulled their children out of school and created a form of home-schooling. The COVID-19 outbreak further entrenched this situation, albeit on a very limited scale. Out of this current, mosque-schools gradually took shape; first established in Qom, they grew rapidly, and today they have branches in 22 provinces and operate under a central headquarters. The number of these schools has doubled over the past 4 years, surpassing 450; with an average of about 30 students per school. After several years of operation, these schools finally obtained operating licenses starting in 1402 as a type of non-governmental school, and they also signed agreements with the government to expand into rural areas. Because these schools use mosque facilities, their tuition is lower, and in addition to more religious instruction, they offer skill-training and income-generation programs; especially income generation through cyberspace and cryptocurrencies.

Alongside this current, a trend of establishing home-schools has also begun in Tehran and is rapidly growing. These are also schools with a student body of between 20 and 40, with very high tuition, often run with supplementary curricula and in more private settings. Many of these home-schools are in practice smaller branches of a private school or affiliated with one. Despite the Ministry of Education's current opposition, these schools do not conflict with the general logic of policymaking in the ministry and face no obstacle to expansion. Home-schools are in the early stages of consolidation, and their activities have so far been reported in some areas of Tehran as well as the metropolises of Tabriz and Isfahan.

The expansion of these micro-schools signals the continuation and intensification of differentiation and the ever-increasing stratification of parts of society into smaller units; a kind of intra-group and intra-class fragmentation. Mosque-schools represent a form of differentiation among more religious families themselves, just as home-schools represent further differentiation among the upper strata of society. These schools should not be conflated with diversity in the educational system, because educational diversity is positive only when it is accompanied by universal access and the possibility of genuine choice for all social groups. Although these schools currently account for a negligible share of the educational system, they are important in terms of institutional analysis.@Omidi_Reza

entry.title: [mamlekate] Exclusive: A US official says Rubio ordered the Iranian delegation to leave…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @mamlekate

Exclusive: A US official says Rubio ordered the Iranian delegation to leave American soil.

According to a US official and another informed source, Marco Rubio, the US Secretary of State, on Monday, after negotiations reached an impasse, asked the delegation of the Islamic Republic of Iran at the United Nations General Assembly to leave the country immediately.

Why does this matter?
Although members of the Iranian delegation were expected to leave American soil soon, Rubio's move is seen as a harsh and unusual diplomatic reaction and, amid futile efforts to end the conflicts, lays bare the depth of mistrust between the two countries.

Qatari mediators tried to untangle the diplomatic knot between Washington and Tehran, but little progress was made, as neither side was willing to back down from its positions.

Among those ordered to leave New York was Abbas Araghchi, Iran's Foreign Minister and Rubio's counterpart.

Account of informed sources
This US official stated: "Marco Rubio expelled the Iranian delegation whose presence had dragged on beyond acceptable limits. The General Assembly was over and it was time for them to go."

What happened behind the scenes?
On Monday morning, the White House hoped that progress would be made in the negotiations with Tehran later in the day; however, by late afternoon it became clear that the negotiations had reached an impasse.

According to this US official, on Monday evening, the United States mission to the United Nations, on Rubio's orders, informed the Iranian mission that Araghchi's accompanying delegation must leave New York immediately.

The Iranian delegation, including Araghchi, headed to the airport a few hours later and left New York for Doha on a flight at 1:20 a.m. Tuesday.

The second source also confirmed that the US had demanded the departure of the Iranian delegation, but noted that Araghchi's travel plan to return to Tehran had already been set for Monday night.

What is the next step?
According to regional sources, Qatari mediators continue consultations with both sides over their proposed compromise plan.

Donald Trump, the US President, on Wednesday, in response to reporters' questions about how to reach an agreement with a government he calls unpredictable, said: "Maybe I'll attack them (blow them up). Maybe I'll target them; we have to make this decision. Either we attack them or we reach an agreement. But the time for this decision is near, and this situation will end very soon, in one way or another."

@mamlekate

I confirm it.

He says this next to the grave of Sayyed Hassan Nasrallah and points out a sturdy man who was Sayyed's bodyguard. He says this sturdy man underwent open-heart surgery after Sayyed's martyrdom. And I remember the dawn of the 10th of Esfand, when I was struggling between life and death.

🔴 Ways to Cultivate Lasting, Real Pleasure in Midlife✍️Mostafa Malekian🔹If someone says, "I just want pleasure," how can we bring them to pleasure? We ask, do you want tea? They say no, I want pleasure. What about reading a book, traveling, or swimming? Again they say no, I just want pleasure. In that case, we have no way to fulfill their desire.But the moment they say, "I like reading books," a path opens up: they can read books and enjoy it.This is the very paradox of pleasure or happiness that John Stuart Mill puts forward: we must want something other than pleasure in order to reach pleasure. Pleasure is the result of attaining something we love.▪️ To be happy, we must attach our hearts to something beyond ourselvesConstant preoccupation with ourselves and with "what should I do to feel better?" can deprive us of the very thing we want. We must find an interest outside ourselves. This attachment takes two forms:First, loving other beings. When we love a person, their happiness makes us happy too. We do something for their comfort and we ourselves enjoy it as well. This affection can be directed toward humans, animals, plants, and other beings.Second, loving the work itself. Let us engage in work we enjoy while doing it; work whose process is dear to us. In that case, we do not postpone enjoyment until the result is reached.▪️ And let us also value the existential values of lifeFood, clothing, housing, sleep, and rest are necessary for the continuation of life; but life does not gain quality merely by meeting these needs. Alongside material values, four other categories of values can enrich life:▫️ Intellectual values: the pleasure of understanding, solving a problem, and finding an answer to a question.▫️ Aesthetic values: communion with nature, literature, and art; experiences that do not necessarily lengthen our lives, but give life quality.▫️ Moral values: humility, honesty, compassion, and love; qualities that can improve the quality of our living.▫️ Spiritual and transcendent values: a sense of oneness with beings, belonging to a transcendent being, and the connection between our own good and harm and that of others; of course, acceptance of this category is not a matter of consensus.To pass through midlife more smoothly, we must give more room to these existential values. Understanding, loving, artistic creation, and kindness, in midlife and beyond, can make our lives more flourishing.📚 Mostafa Malekian | A lecture about the book "Philosophical Guidance for Midlife"@mostafamalekian

entry.title: [jalaeipour] Today's Iranian media have headlined this sentence from the President's speech…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @jalaeipour

Today's Iranian media have headlined this sentence from the President's speech at the annual summit of the "West Asia Union": This year, for the first time in West Asia, extreme poverty was eradicated, and we have no hungry, homeless, out-of-school, or treatment-deprived people. I remember all the years we longed to read such a headline. I remember all the elections in which we pushed to make the eradication of extreme poverty a slogan and a priority for the candidates, and twice it happened, but sanctions, war, and misgovernance prevented its full realization. The deep smile of satisfaction that reading this headline has brought to my lips—I cannot hide it on the metro. The unknown old man across from me, wearing a beautiful Kurdish outfit, smiles too upon seeing my smile. We are immersed in the sweetness of our smiles when my daughter calls from Lark, and her image appears on my smart glasses. Simultaneously with the West Asia Union summit, the Hormuz Festival has been held on the islands of Hormuz, Hengam, and Lark. For several years now, it has brought together the best musicians and the most beautiful clothing and artistic rituals of the residents around the Persian Gulf and thousands of participants from across Iran and the Persian Gulf and other countries, and it has become the most popular art festival of the Global South. The presence of any smart robot at the festival is not permitted, and this very rule has made the ecomuseums of these islands more attractive to young people. My daughter, along with two of her classmates, has gone to participate in the festival by electric high-speed train to Bandar Abbas and from there by electric ship to Lark. She is excited about the beauty of the beaches and the art of the participants and the joy of socializing with friends she discovered at this same festival last year. In a three-dimensional video call from Lark, as last year, she insists that we not stay in Tehran and migrate to Hengam Island. Enthusiastically, she recounts that at iftar in the Shahid Tangsiri Mosque of Lark, shrimp do-piazeh and halva were hosted by the locals. She says: "Dad, just let go of Tehran already! Isn't it a shame to miss even a single day of walking along the shore to watch the sunrise or sunset or the moon?" As it happens, her mother and I have had this same wish for years, and since the beginning of our acquaintance and love, our most beautiful memories and experiences have been tied to the islands around Qeshm and the coasts of Hormozgan, but since the time of Corona and then the wars of 1404 and 1405 and the eventful years after, we were forced to stay and help in Tehran. Now that we see our Iran has flourished and for several years has remained the connecting ring of the world, green and safe, and Samaneh's design and my party work and attendance in the girl's classes at Shahid Minab High School can all be followed in cyberspace, perhaps the time has come to act on her suggestion. An imaginary page from the diary of 8 Mehr 1421@jalaeipour

entry.title: [fazelimohammadir] Gentlemen in charge! A society squeezed economically by war, sanctions, and…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @fazelimohammadir

Gentlemen in charge! A society squeezed economically by war, sanctions, and siege becomes more sensitive, more on edge, and more vulnerable. The smallest social friction in such an environment carries a far higher cost than under normal conditions. A family grappling with inflation, job insecurity, anxiety over medicine, housing, and their children's future has far less capacity to absorb new tensions. At this point, the quality of social policy is directly linked to the country's ability to navigate the crisis. Every policy must be measured by a simple question: Does this policy, at this moment, strengthen social bonds or further inflame existing fractures? Provocative identity debates, cultural disputes such as hijab, the proposal to lash a female singer, the widespread criminalization of social behavior, measures that pit parts of society against other parts, and the reopening of cases like women's dress code are not merely cultural or legal matters. Under crisis conditions, these policies carry a secondary consequence as well: they divert part of society's political, disciplinary, and psychological energy away from the main problem and activate divisions that — you must accept — Iranian society has moved past and the people deserve respect for, yet under economic pressure these divisions have the potential to turn into social fractures. In this sense, a country in crisis needs something akin to a "social ceasefire" — meaning preventing the creation of conflicts that are not urgent and that can drain the country's limited social capital.

spectatorindex White House agreement on artificial intelligence

Joint commitment on accountability for frontier models

To build a hopeful future for the people of America and around the world, we believe that every company has a duty to develop its technology safely and in a way that builds trust with customers and the general public.

The starting point on this path is that all companies engaged in training and deploying frontier models must have strong internal control processes and mechanisms in place to ensure that their technology performs in line with defined objectives and that any potential flaw is immediately identified and addressed. Therefore, in addition to the usual precautionary measures, we believe that every company must implement the following four layers of oversight and auditing:

1. Implementation of rigorous internal control mechanisms to monitor the capabilities and alignment of models during the training and deployment stages, particularly in areas such as cybersecurity, biosecurity, and chemical threats, and to ensure that systems do not engage in intrusion or unauthorized and unintended access to technical infrastructure.

2. Delegation of authority to an internal team to ensure that all control, oversight, and detection systems operate in accordance with established standards and that identified disruptions are resolved without delay.

3. Cooperation with independent external evaluators and auditors to conduct impartial inspections of the correctness of oversight, monitoring, and error detection processes.

4. Appointment of an independent committee drawn from board members for high-level oversight, receiving periodic reports from executive teams and internal and external auditors, and ensuring the complete resolution of all reported deficiencies.

Together, these steps will provide lasting reassurance to companies, customers, and society that the technology in question performs reliably and in line with its original objectives.

Companies that are members of this agreement will meet regularly to develop standards and best practices for enhancing the safety of their systems.

Over time, codifying these mechanisms within the framework of formal laws or regulations will be a logical approach. entry.title: [jalaeipour] Gentlemen in charge! A society that has been economically squeezed by war,…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @jalaeipour

Gentlemen in charge! A society that has been economically squeezed by war, sanctions, and siege becomes more sensitive, more on edge, and more vulnerable. The smallest social conflict in such an atmosphere carries a far higher cost than under normal conditions. A family grappling with inflation, job insecurity, anxiety over medicine, housing, and their children's future has far less capacity to endure new tensions. At this point, the quality of social policy is directly tied to the country's capacity to pull through the crisis. Every policy must be measured against a simple question: Does this policy, at this moment, strengthen social bonds or further inflame existing fractures? Provocative identity debates, cultural disputes such as hijab, the proposal to lash a female singer, the widespread criminalization of social behaviors, actions that set parts of society against other parts, and the reopening of cases such as how women dress are not merely a cultural or legal matter. Under crisis conditions, these policies carry a secondary consequence as well: they divert part of society's political, disciplinary, and psychological energy away from the main problem and activate divisions that you must accept Iranian society has moved past and that the people must be respected for — yet under economic pressure, these divisions have the potential to become a social fracture. In this sense, a country in crisis needs something akin to a "social ceasefire" — meaning preventing the creation of conflicts that are not urgent and that can drain the country's limited social capital.

entry.title:
[bamotamem] National Wealth Fund
This Oxford Handbook on sovereign wealth funds has gotten…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @bamotamem

National Wealth Fund

This Oxford Handbook on sovereign wealth funds has gotten a bit dated (2017). Especially in the financial and investment industry, which has seen rapid changes. But its structure, the framework it offers, and the points it makes about the architecture of sovereign wealth funds are truly excellent.

You probably know that one of the most famous funds belongs to Norway, where the government saves and invests oil revenues through a mechanism. They call it an intergenerational perspective. Their government says the state has no right to spend oil money recklessly, because it also belongs to future generations.

They started thirty years ago. Now it's around 2,400 billion dollars. That's roughly half a million dollars per Norwegian.

Interestingly, nearly 70 percent of this money is the returns generated by the oil money itself that have been added to the fund. In one chapter of this book, it examines this fund's policies, which was interesting. One of them is that they never take more than a 10% stake (with voting rights) in any company, so they don't have to get involved in the day-to-day affairs of companies. It should just be an investment and they take their money.

From this perspective, they differ from approaches like Saudi Arabia's (PIF), which uses national money to buy large stakes in companies.

Iran is facing weeks and months fraught with peril — a period that, at the macro-structural and regional level, could lay the tracks for the collective destiny of all of us and of generations to come. The price Iran pays to get through this bottleneck depends, among other things, on the cohesion, problem-solving capacity, and performance of the entire body of Iran's leaders and influential social and political forces, on the state of every component of national power, and on the horizon that the majority envisions for the years ahead.

I'm talking to you! You, the member of parliament who, in these very weeks, won't even pass up the impeachment of two ministers who serve as custodians of two vital pillars of national resilience! You, the director and editor-in-chief at IRIB who, in these very months, won't steer the national broadcaster toward becoming more genuinely national and more inclusive! You, the planner of the podium for Tehran's main squares who, even in these weeks, won't take any effective step toward making the gatherings in those squares more pluralistic and more unifying! You, the political and civic activist who, even at a juncture like this, remain captive to the game of blame and fault-finding and backward-looking quarrels, effectively prioritizing not the strengthening of national cohesion and resilience but the hunting of pretexts for internal strife and factional posturing! You, the high-ranking official in any of the three branches or public institutions who has failed to make helping the economic war command center and blunting the impact of the siege your most urgent priority — and who still makes decisions as if we were in peacetime, without siege! You, the decision-maker and opinion-shaper who, even after the three recent wars and after hearing Netanyahu's speech and Trump's threat of civilizational destruction at the UN General Assembly, still cannot grasp the imperatives and priorities of a situation in which Iran faces an existential threat — nor what it takes to bring the war to a durable end! You, the judge, the manager, the media figure, the fellow citizen — at whatever level you wield influence — who even in these days is engaged in actions and words and decisions that, instead of building a more hopeful horizon and stronger solidarity, anger part of society, activate divisions, and diminish some people's hope for the future!

I'm talking to you! You too are aboard this same ship — the ship of Iran! The same ship your children will remain aboard in this turbulent region, and for whose protection hundreds of thousands of precious lives and years have already been sacrificed! Our fates are bound together! Every single hour of these days must be spent with the utmost focus and energy on strengthening the foundations and resources of national power and resilience — and on passing through the enormous vortex ahead at the lowest possible cost. Every single hour! Iran is caught up in a great game. Its stakes are far beyond your short-term interests! Don't you want to open your eyes and gain some higher national perspective for a while? @jalaeipour

According to this map, 1,287 of the 1,530 recorded locations were reported during the first 40 days of the war, while only 13 were recorded between April 9 and June 7; then, in June and July, another wave of attacks emerged with 226 reported locations, 138 of which were in southern Iran, in areas below the 30th parallel. Meanwhile, areas such as Bushehr, Bandar Abbas, and Qeshm, which had been targeted before, once again stood out in the data from the second period. Of the total 1,530 cases, 544 are classified as confirmed airstrikes, 550 as reported attacks, and 436 as explosions captured on video; however, in 1,142 cases, the perpetrator of the attack is not identified in the published data. This dataset merely offers a picture of the geographic and temporal distribution of reported cases and, on its own, cannot show the extent of human and civilian damage from any given attack.@sahandiranmehr

entry.title: [hesmashena] I suspect it is precisely at this point that the headline can outrun the text.…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @hesmashena

I suspect it is precisely at this point that the headline can outrun the text. The core message is not necessarily that Iran is more powerful than America, China, or any other power. The core message is that Iran today, in the narrative being presented, is not an Iran that can be dragged back to its former position of dependency. This is no small distinction. In the text, three temporal planes are woven together: a past that must not return, a present that must be defended, and a future that must be more powerful than the present. That is why the message does not conclude in the past either; it moves toward the future. But it is precisely here that the most difficult question begins. "We will not go back" is not merely a statement about a foreign enemy. Not going back cannot be measured solely by missile range, the distance of enemy warships, or military operational capacity. If we take the concept of power seriously, then the economy, knowledge, technology, the quality of governance, public trust, human capital, social cohesion, and the ability to solve problems are all part of that same arena. A country that does not want to go back must be able to simultaneously withstand external threats and, on the domestic front, create the capacity for a better life, greater hope, and the possibility of broader progress. This is where the narrative of power meets people's everyday experience. The narrower the gap between the two, the more the phrase "we will not go back" transforms from a political slogan into a collective experience. The wider this gap grows, the less the foreign enemy even needs to challenge the narrative; people's daily lives will do it for them. The recent message can be read from various angles. One can debate its claim to power, the Strait of Hormuz, regional resistance, or its religious symbolism. But the thread binding all these elements together is, to my mind, too clear to be lost in noisy headlines: "The enemy wants Iran to return to the past; the text says that past is over." The question of Iran's future lies in exactly the same place: let us not go back — not only in independence and security, but in every component that truly makes a nation powerful.

entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @darvishnameh

🔶 Mohammad Darvish: Desalinating Oman Sea water is choosing between bad and worse

The government of Masoud Pezeshkian inaugurated the first phase of the project to transfer water from the Oman Sea to the Central Plateau on the 15th of Azar — a plan that Isfahan's industries see as a lifesaver, but some experts warn about its environmental consequences, its energy intensity, and the threat it poses to the Makran coast.

In this context, Mohammad Darvish, an environmental activist, stressed in an interview with Deutsche Welle Persian that "implementing the desalination project for the Oman Sea and transferring water to Isfahan could have far fewer adverse environmental and security consequences than implementing projects to transfer water from the headwaters of the Karun and Dez to Isfahan."

He added: "Unfortunately, the insistence on carrying out projects such as Cheshmeh Langan and Khodangestan and drying up two headwaters of the Dez River, pursuing destructive projects such as the Mandegan Dam and diverting the Marbor River from the headwaters of the Karun, the Khersan 3 Dam and the Beheshtabad project, the plan to transfer water from the Zayandeh Rud to Yazd, and drawing water from the Zayandeh Rud to develop certain orchards have dealt the biggest blow to the resilience of the Dez, Karun, and Zayandeh Rud watersheds and have fueled widespread discontent in the region."

Darvish concludes that "desalinating sea water itself has worrisome environmental consequences, but when choosing between bad and worse, it is preferable."

At the same time, this environmental activist warns that "this water should not be spent on further industrial development and implementing more projects in Isfahan," and adds: "Additional pressure on the provinces of Isfahan, Yazd, and Markazi in the form of polluting and water-intensive industries must be stopped."

Many independent experts point out that Iran's water crisis will not be solved by transferring new resources. If consumption management is not reformed, if water-intensive agriculture does not change its practices, and if water-intensive industries are not relocated from arid regions, even the largest water transfer projects will only buy time and deepen the current crisis.

@dw_farsi

What are the consequences of fabricated polarizations for Iran?🔹Reducing the country's complex issues to binaries like "peace-seeking vs. warmongering" or "negotiation vs. war" can steer society away from a genuine conversation about national interests, costs, and foreign policy options.🔹Critics of this approach argue that negotiation should be a tool of foreign policy, not the only solution; just as defense and deterrence capabilities should not be equated with "warmongering."🔹The experience of the JCPOA and America's withdrawal from it has brought into sharper focus the debate over guaranteeing an agreement's implementation, reciprocal concessions, and preserving bargaining power. From this perspective, the core issue is not "negotiation or war," but preserving the power of choice and securing national interests.🔹False polarizations, rather than strengthening national cohesion, can deepen social divides; whereas in the face of external threats, internal cohesion, defense capability, economic strength, and active diplomacy can all serve national interests simultaneously.🔹Analysts believe that negotiation can help secure national interests when it is pursued from a position of choice, not out of compulsion and necessity. The experience of past agreements has also shown that an agreement alone, without guarantees of implementation and bargaining power, does not necessarily lead to a sustainable outcome.🔹When individuals and factions are categorized with labels like "warmonger" or "peacenik," the possibility of rational dialogue about details diminishes.🔹From the perspective of critics of polarization, a society that can discuss its differences while emphasizing shared national interests will have a greater capacity to manage foreign crises.@Farspolitics - link

entry.title:
[miladdokhanchi] Let us revive leadership!
Within each of us dwells a sultan and a shepherd.…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @miladdokhanchi

Let us revive leadership!

Within each of us dwells a sultan and a shepherd. The sultan rules and controls; the inner shepherd guides. The sultan leans toward subjugation, domination, and the management of affairs, while the shepherd leans toward guidance, opening new horizons, and stepping into the unknown.

In the language of business, the inner sultan manages and the shepherd leads. The sultan is necessary for managing affairs; the shepherd, for creation, bringing forth, and breaking down the walls of human limitation. Sultanhood gravitates toward the individual; shepherdliness, toward the collective.

In the duality of sultan and shepherd, the question is not one of preference but of balance — and balance becomes possible when we have not only erected the apparatuses of our inner sultanate but also passed beyond them and brought inner leadership into emergence. Yes, both the sultan and the shepherd are needed, but if we are to envision an ultimate destination, that destination is the passage from the inner sultanate to the inner shepherdliness.

Shepherdliness and leadership, then, are not a position. Leadership is a particular way of thinking and being; leadership is a path — in the first instance a personal path that then becomes determinate outwardly and takes on a collective form. The question: shepherd or sultan?

In the process leading to the Islamic Revolution, Iranian society managed to pass beyond sultanate and activate its inner shepherd — and it was this discovered inner shepherd that emerged outwardly, and from its heart, the concept of "Imam" was born. In Iran, leadership emerged because every human being saw themselves as a leader; because leadership emerged as a way of being; because an inner revolution took place in our inner states, and this caused leadership as a collective matter to also appear in Article 43 of the Constitution: "The organization of the country's economic program... such that every individual... has sufficient ability to participate actively in the leadership of the country..."

But in post-revolutionary Iran, leadership was reduced to a position. Once again our inner sultanic relations were activated, and we were degraded from leaders who discovered "leaders" to followers who merely follow. From then on, following, imitation, and the rejection of responsibility became our common behavioral currency. Everywhere: politics, art, culture, economy...

To solve Iran's problems, each of us must first and once again become a leader. We must pass beyond our inner sultanates and activate our inner shepherds; and it is these inner shepherds that, when actualized, make shepherdliness possible outwardly. Without leadership as a plural matter, political and social leadership is also impossible; what emerges without it is not leadership — it is the same sultan wearing the shepherd's clothing.

Let us activate our inner shepherd.

Let us all be leaders.

#Government_Addiction

entry.title: [ahmadzeidabad] Mud-slinging? Sheikh Hamid Rasaei, protesting his ten-month prison sentence,…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @ahmadzeidabad

Mud-slinging? Sheikh Hamid Rasaei, protesting his ten-month prison sentence, wrote a letter of objection — and Tasnim News Agency labeled it "mud-slinging against a judicial ruling" and treated it as a crime! Setting aside any judgment about the form and content of Mr. Rasaei's sentence or whether his protest letter is accurate or not, the way Tasnim News Agency has inserted itself into this affair is wrong on every count. It's as if, in this news agency's view, every judicial ruling is inherently just — even sacred — and any criticism or objection to it amounts to mud-slinging and a crime! Every day, across the entire country, thousands of judicial rulings are issued by different judges, and one of the parties to the dispute considers it unjust and tyrannical and objects to it. Are all of them committing mud-slinging and a crime? The head of the judiciary, under Article 477 of the Criminal Procedure Code, identifies several judicial rulings each month as clearly contrary to Sharia and refers them to the Supreme Court for retrial. Should the head of the judiciary's determination that a judicial ruling clearly contradicts Sharia standards be considered mud-slinging against a judicial ruling and a criminal act? Judges are human too, and even if they care about fairness and justice, they may issue a wrong ruling for thousands of reasons. Meanwhile, some of them have no concern for justice at all and are mired in the very same corruption that afflicts other employees of various institutions! The clearest, most undeniable example is Saeed Mortazavi, who for a time held sway over people's lives, property, and reputation, and in the end the country's highest officials themselves branded him a liar and removed him from office. Unfortunately, during his tenure, the possibility of safe and free criticism of his rulings — by this very logic of Tasnim News Agency — did not exist, and this gave him such an ironclad immunity that he imagined himself all-powerful, and it ultimately ended in the Kahrizak disaster! And yet, someone worse than Saeed Mortazavi still exists, but those same false immunities prevent the country's community of legal experts from criticizing their rulings. In any case, the mindset of the likes of Tasnim News Agency unfortunately does nothing to help reform and improve the judiciary's performance, no matter who the other party may be. The purpose of this piece is not to judge the nature of Mr. Rasaei's sentence or to defend his actions, which in my view are mostly sensationalist and wrong. The aim is to defend his right to object to his sentence — a right that is natural and God-given, and that even current laws recognize for every single citizen, whatever their station, yet it seems some are trying to take it away. #احمد_زیدآبادی @ahmadzeidabad
